bigOGrowth.title: How Big O grows
bigOGrowth.constant: O(1): the line stays flat. The work doesn't grow with n.
bigOGrowth.log: O(log n): grows very slowly. Doubling n adds only one more step.
bigOGrowth.linear: O(n): a straight line. Twice the input means twice the work.
bigOGrowth.quadratic: O(n²): shoots up. At n = 1,000 it's already 1,000,000 operations.
bigOGrowth.summary: From best to worst: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n²).
bigOGrowth.nLogN: O(n log n): a bit steeper than O(n), and far below O(n²). Good sorting algorithms land here.
bigOGrowth.sortTitle: Where sort fits: O(n log n)
bigOGrowth.sortSummary: sort is O(n log n): slower than one pass over the array, much faster than comparing every pair.

arrayReindex.title: Array operations and re-indexing
arrayReindex.start: Every guest in the array has an index, starting at 0.
arrayReindex.push: push('Eli') adds to the end. No other guest moves: O(1).
arrayReindex.pop: pop() removes from the end. No other guest moves: O(1).
arrayReindex.shift: shift() removes the first guest, so every other guest moves down one index: O(n).
arrayReindex.unshift: unshift('Ana') adds to the start, so every guest moves up one index: O(n).

binarySearch.title: Binary search: cut the list in half
binarySearch.start: Find '{{target}}' in a guest list of {{count}} names sorted A to Z.
binarySearch.goRight: The middle name is '{{middle}}', which comes before '{{target}}' in ABC order: throw away the left half.
binarySearch.goLeft: The middle name is '{{middle}}', which comes after '{{target}}' in ABC order: throw away the right half.
binarySearch.found: Found '{{target}}' after {{checks}} checks. log₂(8) = 3: that's O(log n).

stopwatchRace.title: Timing the same code on two computers
stopwatchRace.start: The same code welcomes {{n}} guests. Let's time it on a fast laptop and an old phone.
stopwatchRace.firstRun: The laptop is much faster… but both did exactly {{n}} steps.
stopwatchRace.secondRun: Run it again: different times! Other apps and the browser change every run. The steps are still {{n}}.
stopwatchRace.moreGuests: Now {{n}} guests. The times change again, but the steps simply doubled to {{n}}.
stopwatchRace.summary: Seconds depend on the machine. Steps depend only on the code and n. Big O counts steps.
stopwatchRace.tooFast: A tiny job (2 guests): both show 0.0 ms. Code this fast can't be measured, so the stopwatch can't tell which version is faster.

searchCases.title: Best, average and worst case
searchCases.start: isInvited reads the list from the start. How much work it does depends on where the name is.
searchCases.best: '{{name}}' is first: found in {{checks}} check. The best case is called Ω (omega).
searchCases.average: '{{name}}' is in the middle: {{checks}} checks. The average case is called Θ (theta).
searchCases.worst: '{{name}}' isn't on the list: all {{checks}} names checked. The worst case is called O: big O.
searchCases.summary: Big O always means the worst case: the code will never be slower than this.

linearBoxes.title: O(n): one step per guest
linearBoxes.chartLabel: Steps grow in a straight line with the number of guests
linearBoxes.eight: Double the guests (8) and the work doubles too: 8 steps.
linearBoxes.line: The dots form a straight line. Work that grows like this is O(n), linear time.

constantJump.title: O(1): jump straight to the box
constantJump.start: The guest list. Each box has an index.
constantJump.jump: guests[3] jumps straight to box 3. No need to look at boxes 0, 1 and 2.
constantJump.length: guests.length is also just one step: the array already knows its size.
constantJump.huge: With a million guests, guests[500000] still jumps straight there: 1 step.
constantJump.summary: The work doesn't change with the size of the list. That's O(1), constant time: the best Big O.

sameShape.title: Drop the constants: same shape
sameShape.n: One loop over the guests: n steps. A straight line.
sameShape.twoN: Two loops in a row: 2n steps. Steeper, but still a straight line.
sameShape.threeN: 3n: steeper again, and still a straight line.
sameShape.nSquared: n² is different: it bends upward and leaves the others behind.
sameShape.summary: n, 2n and 3n have the same shape, so they are all O(n). We drop the constant.

nestedGrid.title: O(n²): every guest greets every guest
nestedGrid.start: Each row is a guest (i). For every row, the inner loop goes through every column (j).
nestedGrid.row: {{guest}}'s row is done: the inner loop ran {{n}} times. Grey cells are a guest meeting themselves (skipped).
nestedGrid.double: Double the guests to {{n}}: {{n}} × {{n}} = {{total}} steps. Twice the guests, 4 times the work!
nestedGrid.summary: A loop inside a loop over the same list is O(n²), quadratic time.

dominantTerm.title: Drop the non-dominant terms
dominantTerm.share: The n part is {{share}}% of the work.
dominantTerm.size: n = {{n}}: n² is {{squared}} and n adds only {{n}} more. The n part is {{share}}% of {{total}}.
dominantTerm.summary: As n grows, n² does almost all the work. So O(n² + n) is written O(n²).

twoInputs.title: Two inputs: guests (a) and helpers (b)
twoInputs.start: The party has 4 guests (a) and 2 helpers (b): two different lists.
twoInputs.guests: First loop: welcome every guest. That's a steps.
twoInputs.helpers: Then a second loop over the helpers: b more steps. In total: O(a + b).
twoInputs.grid: Now every guest thanks every helper: a loop over helpers inside a loop over guests. That's a × b steps: O(a · b).
twoInputs.summary: Don't call both sizes n: there could be 4 guests and 1,000 helpers. Use one letter per input.

memoryBoxes.title: Space: how much memory grows?
memoryBoxes.counter: Counting {{n}} guests only needs one box: the counter.
memoryBoxes.counterBig: With {{n}} guests it's still one box. O(1) space.
memoryBoxes.tags: Making a name tag for each of {{n}} guests needs a new box per guest.
memoryBoxes.tagsBig: {{n}} guests → {{n}} name tags. The memory grows with n: O(n) space.
memoryBoxes.summary: Space complexity counts the extra memory the code creates as the input grows.

halvingCount.title: Logarithms count halvings
halvingCount.start: 16 boxes. How many times can we cut them in half until 1 is left?
halvingCount.one: Only 1 left after {{halvings}} halvings. So log₂(16) = 4.
halvingCount.big: 1,024 boxes need only 10 halvings, and a million need about 20. That's why O(log n) is so fast.

isInvited.title: isInvited: stop as soon as you find the name
isInvited.start: Is '{{name}}' on the list of {{count}} guests? Start at i = 0.
isInvited.noMatch: Is guests[{{i}}] ('{{guest}}') equal to '{{name}}'? No → keep going.
isInvited.match: guests[{{i}}] is '{{guest}}'. Found it! Return true after {{ops}} checks.
isInvited.notFound: The loop ended: '{{name}}' isn't on the list. Return false after {{ops}} checks.

isInvitedAll.title: isInvitedAll: always read the whole list
isInvitedAll.start: Is '{{name}}' on the list of {{count}} guests? found starts as false.
isInvitedAll.match: guests[{{i}}] is '{{name}}': found = true… but the loop doesn't stop!
isInvitedAll.keepReading: '{{guest}}': we already found the name, but we keep reading anyway.
isInvitedAll.end: Return {{found}} after {{ops}} checks: every guest, every time.

countShortNames.title: Counting operations
countShortNames.loopCheck: Is i ({{i}}) < {{n}}? Yes, so the loop runs again: one operation.
countShortNames.isShort: '{{guest}}' has {{length}} letters, 3 or fewer: one operation for the check…
countShortNames.isLong: '{{guest}}' has {{length}} letters, more than 3: one operation for the check.
countShortNames.addOne: …and one for count = count + 1 (now {{count}}). Then i++ is one more.
countShortNames.fastForward: With {{n}} guests we skip to the end. Each guest costs 3 or 4 operations.
countShortNames.end: Done: {{ops}} operations for {{n}} guests. Try the other sizes: the total grows with n.

welcomeAll.title: welcomeAll: one message per guest
welcomeAll.start: Welcome {{n}} guests, one at a time.
welcomeAll.end: {{n}} guests → {{n}} messages. The work grows with n: O(n).

welcomeAndGoodbye.title: Two loops in a row
welcomeAndGoodbye.start: First welcome every guest, then say goodbye to every guest.
welcomeAndGoodbye.secondLoop: The first loop is done ({{n}} messages). Now the second loop starts.
welcomeAndGoodbye.end: {{n}} + {{n}} = {{total}} messages: 2n. Drop the constant: it's still O(n).

greetEveryone.title: greetEveryone: a loop inside a loop
greetEveryone.start: For each guest i, the inner loop goes through every guest j.
greetEveryone.self: i and j are both {{a}}: you don't greet yourself, but the inner loop still took a step.

partySummary.title: Rules of thumb: the cost of each line
partySummary.index: guests[0]: reading by index is one step. O(1).
partySummary.math: guests.length + 2: math on numbers is O(1), however big the numbers are.
partySummary.assign: let longNames = 0: giving a variable a value is O(1).
partySummary.inside: Inside the loop: one check and maybe one addition. O(1) each time…
partySummary.loop: …but the loop runs n times. Cost of a loop = times it runs × work inside = n × O(1) = O(n).
partySummary.total: Add it up: O(1) + O(1) + O(1) + O(n) + O(1). Drop the small terms: O(n).

countGuests.title: Counting every operation
countGuests.init: let count = 0: giving a variable a value is 1 operation.
countGuests.startLoop: let i = 0: 1 more operation. It runs only once, when the loop starts.
countGuests.compare: Is i ({{i}}) < {{n}}? A comparison: 1 operation. Yes, so the loop runs.
countGuests.add: count = count + 1: an addition and an assignment, 2 operations. count is now {{count}}.
countGuests.next: i++ is short for i = i + 1: 2 more operations. Back to the comparison.
countGuests.fastForward: With {{n}} guests we jump to the end. Every guest costs the same 5 operations.
countGuests.end: {{ops}} operations to count {{n}} guests: 5 per guest plus 3, or 5n + 3. guests.length gives the same answer ({{count}}) in 1 step.

giveGifts.title: A loop with a limit
giveGifts.start: {{n}} guests are on the list, but only the first 5 get a gift.
giveGifts.limit: i is {{i}}, so i < 5 is false: the loop stops, even though {{left}} guests are left.
giveGifts.noMoreGuests: No more guests: the loop ends before reaching the limit.
giveGifts.end: {{gifts}} gifts for {{n}} guests. Pick 20 guests: still 5. The loop never runs more than 5 times, so it's O(1).

sumLoop.title: sumUpTo: add the numbers one by one
sumLoop.init: let total = 0: 1 operation. It happens once, whatever n is.
sumLoop.startLoop: let i = 1: 1 more operation, also only once.
sumLoop.compare: Is i ({{i}}) <= n ({{n}})? A comparison: 1 operation. Yes, so the loop runs.
sumLoop.add: total = total + {{i}}: an addition and an assignment, 2 operations. total is now {{total}}. Then i++ adds 2 more.
sumLoop.fastForward: With n = {{n}} we skip to the end: every number costs the same 5 operations.
sumLoop.end: The sum of 1 to {{n}} is {{total}}, after {{ops}} operations: 5n + 2. The bigger n is, the more work.

sumFormula.title: sumUpToFormula: one formula, no loop
sumFormula.start: The same question for n = {{n}}, answered with a formula instead of a loop.
sumFormula.end: The sum of 1 to {{n}} is {{value}}, in 3 operations. Try n = 1,000,000: still 3.

printNumbers.title: printNumbers: n in, n lines out
printNumbers.start: Give the function n = {{n}}. The loop goes from i = 0 while i < {{n}}.
printNumbers.end: We passed in {{n}} and it ran {{n}} times: {{n}} lines. That's O(n).

printPairs.title: printPairs: a loop inside a loop
printPairs.start: For every i, the inner loop goes through every j.

doubleArray.title: doubleArray: a new array that grows
doubleArray.start: doubled starts as an empty array. It's new memory the function creates.
doubleArray.end: {{n}} numbers in, {{n}} new boxes of memory. The extra memory grows with n: O(n) space.

hasAnswer.title: hasAnswer: look for a value, answer by answer
hasAnswer.start: Did anyone answer '{{answer}}'? Object.keys gives us the {{count}} names to loop over.
hasAnswer.match: {{name}} answered '{{answer}}'. Found it! Return true after {{ops}} checks.
hasAnswer.notFound: The loop ended: nobody answered '{{answer}}'. Return false after {{ops}} checks.

charCount.title: charCount, the simple version, character by character
charCount.start: charCount('{{text}}'): an empty object to fill and {{count}} characters to read.
charCount.firstTime: {{char}} isn't a key yet: result[{{char}}] is undefined, and undefined > 0 is false. Set it to 1.
charCount.again: {{char}} is already a key, so add 1. It's at {{count}} now.
charCount.done: All {{ops}} characters read, in one pass: O(n). The object has {{keys}} keys.

linkedListWalk.title: Walking the line with temp
linkedListWalk.start: temp starts where head points: {{name}}. We move temp, never head.
linkedListWalk.startEmpty: The line is empty. head is null, so temp starts as null too.
linkedListWalk.greet: temp isn't null, so the loop runs: say hi to {{name}}.
linkedListWalk.move: temp = temp.next moves temp one node forward, to {{name}}.
linkedListWalk.moveToNull: temp = temp.next: {{name}} was the last guest, so temp is null now.
linkedListWalk.stop: temp is null, so the loop stops. Nodes visited: {{count}}. Walking the list is O(n).

linkedListConstructor.title: The LinkedList constructor, line by line
linkedListConstructor.head: Start empty: this.head = null.
linkedListConstructor.tail: this.tail = null: there's no last node yet either.
linkedListConstructor.length: this.length = 0. This is already a valid, empty list.
linkedListConstructor.noValue: value is undefined: nothing was passed in. The if is skipped, and the list stays empty.
linkedListConstructor.emptyDone: Done: an empty list. head and tail are null and length is 0. push can add guests later.
linkedListConstructor.hasValue: value is {{value}}, not undefined, so we make the first node.
linkedListConstructor.zero: value is 0. That's not undefined, so 0 gets a node like any other value.
linkedListConstructor.nodeValue: new Node({{value}}) runs the Node constructor: this.value = {{value}}.
linkedListConstructor.nodeNext: this.next = null: the new node doesn't point anywhere yet. newNode points to it.
linkedListConstructor.pointHead: this.head = newNode: head points to the new node.
linkedListConstructor.pointTail: this.tail = this.head: tail points to the same node as head. One node, two pointers.
linkedListConstructor.done: this.length = 1. A list with one node: head and tail are both on {{value}}.

linkedListPush.title: push, line by line
linkedListPush.newNode: new Node('{{value}}') makes the new node, and newNode points to it. It isn't in the line yet.
linkedListPush.empty: !this.head is true: head is null, and null is falsy. The line is empty.
linkedListPush.emptyHead: this.head = newNode: the new node is the first guest...
linkedListPush.emptyTail: this.tail = newNode: ...and the last one. head and tail share it.
linkedListPush.notEmpty: !this.head is false: head is on {{head}}, so we skip to the else.
linkedListPush.link: this.tail.next = newNode: tail is on {{tail}}, so {{tail}}'s next now points to {{value}}.
linkedListPush.moveTail: this.tail = newNode: tail moves to {{value}}, the new last guest.
linkedListPush.return: return this gives back the whole list. No walking at all: push is O(1).

linkedListUnshift.title: unshift, line by line
linkedListUnshift.newNode: new Node('{{value}}') makes the new node, and newNode points to it. It isn't in the line yet.
linkedListUnshift.empty: !this.head is true: head is null, and null is falsy. The line is empty.
linkedListUnshift.emptyHead: this.head = newNode: the new node is the first guest...
linkedListUnshift.emptyTail: this.tail = newNode: ...and the last one. head and tail share it.
linkedListUnshift.notEmpty: !this.head is false: head is on {{head}}, so we skip to the else.
linkedListUnshift.link: newNode.next = this.head: {{value}} now points to {{head}}, the first guest. Link first, so nobody gets lost.
linkedListUnshift.moveHead: this.head = newNode: head moves to {{value}}, the new first guest.
linkedListUnshift.return: return this gives back the whole list. Two moves and no walking: unshift is O(1).

linkedListPop.title: pop, line by line
linkedListPop.empty: !this.head is true: the line is empty, so there's nothing to pop.
linkedListPop.returnUndefined: return undefined. The list doesn't change.
linkedListPop.notEmpty: !this.head is false: head is on {{name}}, so there's a guest to pop.
linkedListPop.start: temp and pre both start at head, on {{name}}.
linkedListPop.movePre: temp.next is {{next}}, not null, so the loop runs. pre = temp: pre moves to {{name}}.
linkedListPop.moveTemp: temp = temp.next: temp moves ahead to {{name}}. pre stays one node behind.
linkedListPop.loopEnds: temp.next is null: temp is on {{name}}, the last node, and pre is on {{pre}}, the one before. The loop stops.
linkedListPop.loopSkipped: temp.next is already null: {{name}} is the only node, so the loop doesn't run at all.
linkedListPop.moveTail: this.tail = pre: tail moves back to {{name}}.
linkedListPop.tailSame: this.tail = pre: tail was already on {{name}}, so nothing changes.
linkedListPop.cut: this.tail.next = null: the new tail stops pointing to {{name}}. {{name}} is out of the line.
linkedListPop.cutNothing: this.tail.next = null: it was already null, so nothing changes. But head and tail still point to {{name}}!
linkedListPop.nowEmpty: length is 0, so the line is empty: head and tail have to let go of the node.
linkedListPop.tailNull: this.tail = null. Now the empty line really looks empty.
linkedListPop.notZero: length is {{length}}, not 0, so the line still has guests. Skip the if.
linkedListPop.return: return temp: {{name}}'s node, the guest who left. Nodes visited: {{count}}. The walk grows with the line, so pop is O(n).

linkedListShift.title: shift, line by line
linkedListShift.empty: !this.head is true: the line is empty, so there's nothing to shift.
linkedListShift.returnUndefined: return undefined. The list doesn't change.
linkedListShift.notEmpty: !this.head is false: head is on {{name}}, so there's a guest to shift.
linkedListShift.temp: let temp = this.head: temp points to {{name}}'s node, so we can return it at the end.
linkedListShift.moveHead: this.head = this.head.next: head moves to {{next}}. {{name}} is out of the line, but still points to {{next}}.
linkedListShift.headNull: this.head = this.head.next: {{name}} had no next, so head is null now.
linkedListShift.cut: temp.next = null: {{name}}'s node lets go of the line, so the node we return comes alone.
linkedListShift.cutNothing: temp.next = null: it was already null, so nothing changes. But tail still points to {{name}}!
linkedListShift.tailNull: length is 0, so this.tail = null. Now head and tail are both null.
linkedListShift.notZero: length is {{length}}, not 0, so tail stays where it is.
linkedListShift.return: return temp: {{name}}'s node. One move of head and no walking: shift is O(1).

linkedListGet.title: get, line by line
linkedListGet.outOfRange: Index {{index}} is out of range: valid indexes go from 0 to {{last}}.
linkedListGet.returnUndefined: return undefined, without walking at all.
linkedListGet.inRange: Index {{index}} is in range: it's at least 0 and below the length, {{length}}.
linkedListGet.start: temp starts at head, on {{name}}: index 0.
linkedListGet.move: temp = temp.next: temp is on {{name}}, index {{at}}.
linkedListGet.return: return temp: {{name}}'s node, index {{index}}. Nodes visited: {{count}}. Finding by index is O(n).

linkedListSet.title: set, line by line
linkedListSet.gotUndefined: this.get({{index}}) returns undefined: there's no index {{index}}.
linkedListSet.notNode: temp is undefined, which is falsy, so the if is skipped.
linkedListSet.gotNode: this.get({{index}}) walks to index {{index}} and returns {{name}}'s node.
linkedListSet.isNode: temp is a node, which is truthy, so the if runs.
linkedListSet.change: temp.value = value: {{old}} becomes {{value}}. Same node, new value.
linkedListSet.returnTrue: return true: the value changed. The walk inside get makes set O(n).

linkedListInsert.title: insert, line by line
linkedListInsert.outOfRange: Index {{index}} is out of range: insert accepts 0 to {{length}}.
linkedListInsert.inRange: Index {{index}} is in range: from 0 to {{length}}.
linkedListInsert.isZero: Index 0 is the front of the line.
linkedListInsert.unshift: this.unshift(value) adds {{value}} at the front, in O(1).
linkedListInsert.returnTrue: return true: {{value}} is in the line.
linkedListInsert.isEnd: Index {{index}} equals the length: the back of the line.
linkedListInsert.push: this.push(value) adds {{value}} at the back, in O(1).
linkedListInsert.middle: Index {{index}} isn't 0 or the length, {{length}}: it goes in the middle.
linkedListInsert.newNode: new Node(value) makes a node for {{value}}.
linkedListInsert.before: this.get({{before}}) walks to {{name}}, the node right before index {{index}}.
linkedListInsert.linkNew: newNode.next = temp.next: {{value}} points to {{next}}, so nobody gets lost.
linkedListInsert.linkBefore: temp.next = newNode: {{name}} points to {{value}}. {{value}} is in, at index {{index}}.

linkedListRemove.title: remove, line by line
linkedListRemove.outOfRange: Index {{index}} is out of range: valid indexes go from 0 to {{last}}.
linkedListRemove.inRange: Index {{index}} is in range: from 0 to {{last}}.
linkedListRemove.isZero: Index 0 is the front of the line.
linkedListRemove.shift: return this.shift(): {{name}}'s node comes off the front and is returned.
linkedListRemove.pop: return this.pop(): {{name}}'s node comes off the back and is returned.
linkedListRemove.middle: Index {{index}} is in the middle: not 0, and not the last index, {{last}}.
linkedListRemove.before: this.get({{before}}) walks to {{name}}, the node before the one that leaves.
linkedListRemove.temp: temp = before.next: {{name}}, the node that leaves. No second walk.
linkedListRemove.skip: before.next = temp.next: {{before}} now points past {{name}}, straight to {{next}}.
linkedListRemove.cut: temp.next = null: {{name}}'s node lets go of {{next}}.
linkedListRemove.return: return temp: {{name}}'s node, on its own. The walk makes remove O(n).

linkedListReverse.title: reverse, line by line
linkedListReverse.temp: temp = this.head: temp remembers the old first node, {{name}}.
linkedListReverse.tempEmpty: temp = this.head: the line is empty, so temp is null.
linkedListReverse.head: this.head = this.tail: head moves to {{name}}, the old last node.
linkedListReverse.headEmpty: this.head = this.tail: both are null, so nothing changes.
linkedListReverse.tail: this.tail = temp: tail moves to {{name}}, the old first node. head and tail have swapped.
linkedListReverse.vars: prev and next start as null. prev will trail behind temp, and next will run ahead of it.
linkedListReverse.remember: next = temp.next: before flipping {{name}}'s arrow, next holds on to {{next}}, the rest of the line.
linkedListReverse.rememberLast: next = temp.next: {{name}} is the last node, so next is null.
linkedListReverse.flipFirst: temp.next = prev: {{name}} now points to null. It's the end of the reversed line.
linkedListReverse.flip: temp.next = prev: {{name}}'s arrow flips to point back at {{prev}}.
linkedListReverse.step: prev = temp and temp = next: prev moves to {{prev}}, and temp crosses the gap to {{temp}}.
linkedListReverse.stepLast: prev = temp and temp = next: prev is on {{prev}}, and temp is null. Every arrow has been flipped.
linkedListReverse.return: return this. Each node was visited once, so it's O(n) time, with just 3 extra pointers: O(1) space.
linkedListReverse.returnEmpty: The loop never ran: an empty line reversed is still empty. return this.

timingChart.title: Timing both versions as n grows
timingChart.start: We time sumUpTo for bigger and bigger n, from 200 million to 1 billion, and put each time on a chart.
timingChart.firstPoint: With n = 200 million, the loop takes about a quarter of a second.
timingChart.loopLine: Each time n grows by 200 million, the time grows by about the same amount. The points line up: a straight line.
timingChart.formula: The formula takes almost no time, whatever n is: a flat line along the bottom.
timingChart.noise: These are example times. Run it on your computer and they'll be a little different, and tiny inputs jump around. What stays the same is the shape.
timingChart.summary: The loop's time grows in a line with n (O(n)); the formula's stays flat (O(1)). Big O names these shapes.

arraySplice.title: Adding and removing in the middle
arraySplice.start: Five guests, each with an index.
arraySplice.insert: splice(1, 0, 'Zoe') puts Zoe at index 1. Ben, Cleo, Dev and Eli all move up one index.
arraySplice.remove: splice(2, 1) removes Ben. Cleo, Dev and Eli all move down one index.
arraySplice.notHalf: In the middle, about half the items move, but it's still O(n): Big O is the worst case (inserting at index 0 moves them all), and ½n drops its constant anyway.

arrayVsObject.title: Two free data structures: an array and an object
arrayVsObject.start: The same party stored two ways. The array keeps the guests in order; the object labels each answer with the guest's name.
arrayVsObject.access: Reading with an index or a key jumps straight to one box. Both are O(1).
arrayVsObject.addEnd: Adding to the end of the array, or adding a new key to the object, touches one box. Both are O(1).
arrayVsObject.addStart: Adding to the start is different. The array has to re-index every guest: O(n). The object has no start, so it still touches one box.
arrayVsObject.search: Searching for something that isn't there means checking every box, in both: O(n).
arrayVsObject.summary: Arrays give you order. Objects give you fast keys but no order. Every data structure is a trade-off like this one.

access.title: Reading a key: one jump
access.start: The answers object: 5 guests, 5 keys. No indexes, and no first or last key.
access.read: rsvps['Dev'] goes straight to Dev's card. It doesn't look at Ana, Ben or Cleo first: 1 box.
access.dot: rsvps.Eli is the same lookup written with a dot. Eli was added last, but that doesn't make it slower.
access.missing: 'Zoe' isn't a key. JavaScript goes straight to where Zoe's card would be, finds nothing and returns undefined: still 1 step.
access.huge: A party of a million guests: rsvps['Zoe'] still jumps straight to Zoe. 1 box, whatever the size.
access.summary: Reading a key is O(1), constant time, just like reading an array by its index.

write.title: Adding, changing and deleting keys
write.add: rsvps['Fay'] = 'yes' adds a new key. No other card moves or changes: O(1).
write.update: Ben changed his mind. Updating is a lookup plus a new value: O(1).
write.remove: delete rsvps['Cleo'] removes one key. Nobody has an index, so nobody is re-indexed: O(1).
write.summary: Adding, changing and deleting each touched one card. Compare that with shift and unshift on an array.

hasKey.title: Is this key there? Is this value there?
hasKey.start: Two questions: is a guest on the list (a key), and did anyone answer 'late' (a value)?
hasKey.has: hasOwnProperty('Dev') jumps to where Dev's key would be. It's there: true. 1 box, O(1).
hasKey.hasNot: hasOwnProperty('Zoe') jumps to where Zoe's key would be. Nothing's there: false. Still 1 step.
hasKey.value: Values have no shortcut. To know if anyone said 'late', every answer has to be read: O(n).
hasKey.summary: Checking for a key is O(1). Searching for a value is O(n).

objectToArray.title: Object.keys builds a new array
objectToArray.start: Object.keys(rsvps) starts with an empty array.
objectToArray.firstKey: It visits the first key, '{{key}}', and copies it into the new array: 1 step.
objectToArray.nextKey: Next key: '{{key}}'. That's {{count}} steps so far.
objectToArray.keysDone: Every key was visited once: {{n}} keys, {{n}} steps and {{n}} new boxes of memory.
objectToArray.values: Object.values takes the same walk, copying the answers instead of the names.
objectToArray.entries: Object.entries copies both, as [key, value] pairs. A bit more work per key, but still one visit per key.
objectToArray.summary: Double the keys and you double the work and the memory: O(n) time and O(n) space.

copies.title: concat, slice and splice: how many boxes?
copies.start: Six guests. Each method below copies or moves some of them. Count the boxes it touches.
copies.concat: concat copies every item of both arrays into a new one: 6 + 3 = 9 boxes. That's O(n + m), which we simply call O(n).
copies.slice: slice(1, 4) copies the items from index 1 up to (but not including) index 4: 3 boxes. The cost is the size of the copy.
copies.sliceAll: slice() with no arguments copies the whole array: all 6 boxes. In the worst case, O(n).
copies.spliceMiddle: splice(2, 0, 'Zoe') inserts Zoe at index 2. Every guest after her moves up one index: 5 boxes.
copies.spliceStart: At index 0, splice moves everyone: 7 boxes. Big O takes this worst case: O(n).
copies.summary: All three grow with the size of the array: O(n).

loops.title: forEach, map, filter and reduce: hidden loops
loops.start: Five guests. Each of these methods runs your function once for every guest.
loops.forEach: forEach visits every guest once to print the name: 5 boxes. It returns nothing.
loops.map: map visits every guest and builds a new array of the same length: 5 visits, 5 new boxes.
loops.filter: filter visits every guest and keeps the ones that pass the test (3-letter names): 5 visits, 4 kept.
loops.reduce: reduce visits every guest and combines them into one value, the total length of their names: {{value}}.
loops.summary: One line each, but each one is a loop over the whole array: O(n).

map.title: The 5 steps for any problem
map.start: A problem you've never seen, and no idea where to start. Here's a plan you can follow every time.
map.understand: Step 1: understand the problem. Before any code, make sure you know what goes in, what comes out and what's missing.
map.examples: Step 2: explore examples. Write a few inputs with the output you expect, from easy ones to strange ones.
map.breakDown: Step 3: break it down. Write the steps as short comments, so you have a direction.
map.solve: Step 4: solve it, or solve a simpler version first and add the hard part back later.
map.lookBack: Step 5: look back and refactor. It works, so now make it clearer, faster, or both.
map.summary: Understand, explore, break it down, solve, look back. You'll use these 5 steps for the rest of the course.

understand.title: Step 1: understand the problem
understand.start: Before writing code, ask five questions: out loud in an interview, or to yourself at home.
items: Can I explain it back in my own words?
Is that enough to get the answer?
notes: Explaining it back in your own words proves you understood it, and catches mistakes before they become code.
Inputs: what goes in, what type it is, how big it can get and how many there are.
Outputs: what comes back, and in what shape: a number, a string, an object?
Sometimes something is missing, like a second number. You may only notice later, and that's fine.
Good names now (add, num1, num2, sum) make every next step easier to talk about.
understand.summary: Five questions, a minute or two. They're the cheapest way to avoid solving the wrong problem.

examples.title: Step 2: explore examples
examples.start: Examples turn a problem written in words into inputs and outputs you can check.
items: Move on to more complex examples
notes: Simple examples first: the easiest inputs, with outputs you're sure about.
Then harder ones: spaces, capital letters, digits. Each one tends to raise a question.
Empty inputs, like '' or []: what should come back?
Invalid inputs, like a number where a string should be: return something, or stop with an error?
examples.summary: Write your examples down. When your code is done, they're the first tests you run.

breakDown.title: Step 3: break it down
breakDown.start: Before the real code, write the steps you'll take, in plain words.
items: Write the main steps as comments
Think about the logic before the syntax
Spot the parts you don't know yet
notes: Not every line, and not real code: just the main steps, as short comments.
Deciding what to do first means you don't fight the syntax and the logic at the same time.
Writing the plan shows the steps you're unsure about, so you can ask about them early.
breakDown.summary: A plan written down is something you can show, check and come back to, even if time runs out.

solve.title: Step 4: solve or simplify
solve.start: Can you solve all of it? Great. If not, solve a simpler problem first.
notes: Find the one part that's tripping you up, like checking whether a character is a letter.
Ignore it for a moment. Simplify the problem, don't change it.
Write a working solution for everything else. Now you have real code to show and to run.
Bring the hard part back. Often the simple version has shown you how to do it.
solve.summary: Some progress beats none, and the simpler problem is often the road into the harder one.

lookBack.title: Step 5: look back and refactor
lookBack.start: It works. Before you stop, ask these questions about your solution.
items: Is there another way to get there?
Can it be faster, or use less memory?
How did other people solve it?
notes: Check the result: run your examples from step 2 again.
There's rarely only one solution. Now that you've solved it once, a second way may be easy to see.
Is it easy to read? Would a teammate understand it on a whiteboard?
Does it look like a problem you've solved before, or one you'll meet later?
Performance: its Big O in time and space. Nested loops are the first thing to look at.
Style: clear names, let and const, the conventions of the language and your team.
Other people's solutions, even in another language, are a great way to learn new tricks.
lookBack.summary: Looking back is where you learn the most. Every problem you review makes the next one easier.

exampleLadder.title: Examples for charCount, from easy to strange
exampleLadder.start: The problem: count how many times each character appears in a string. Let's write examples before any code.
exampleLadder.row0: 'aaa' is easy: one character, three times. The output is an object: { a: 3 }.
exampleLadder.row1: 'banana' is still easy, and shows the shape of the answer: one key per character, with its count.
exampleLadder.row2: 'Hi Ana!' raises questions. Do we count the space? The '!'? Are 'H' and 'h' the same letter?
exampleLadder.row3: 'Party at 8!' adds a digit. Should '8' be counted?
exampleLadder.row4: An empty string: return an empty object, or something else?
exampleLadder.row5: A number instead of a string: return something, or stop with an error?
exampleLadder.decided: Our answers: count letters and digits only, in lowercase, and accept only strings. Each answer came from an example.
exampleLadder.onlyStrings: Not a string: we only accept strings

stepsToCode.title: From a plan in comments to code
stepsToCode.start: First, the plan: six comments and no code. This is what you'd write before anything else.

comments.loop: loop over the string, one character at a time
comments.addOne: a letter or digit that's already a key: add 1
comments.setOne: a letter or digit that's not a key yet: set it to 1

stepsToCode.makeObject: The easy part first: an empty object, result, to fill and return.
stepsToCode.loop: The loop over the string. We lowercase each character as we read it, so 'H' and 'h' count together.
stepsToCode.addOne: A character that's already a key gets 1 more. isAlphaNumeric doesn't exist yet: we gave the step a name and kept going.
stepsToCode.setOne: A new letter or digit starts at 1.
stepsToCode.skip: Spaces and punctuation: nothing to do, so all that's left is to close the if and the loop.
stepsToCode.returnIt: Return the object. Every comment now has its code.
stepsToCode.summary: The comments were the plan, and the plan became the code. Only isAlphaNumeric is left to write.

solutionLayers.title: Solve a simpler problem, then add the hard parts back
solutionLayers.simple: Layer 1: the simple charCount. It ignores case and doesn't check what kind of character it reads.
solutionLayers.simpleOutput: On 'Hi Ana!' it runs, but 'H' and 'A' are counted apart from 'h' and 'a', and the space and '!' are counted too.
solutionLayers.lowercase: Layer 2: one change. Each character is lowercased as we read it.
solutionLayers.lowercaseOutput: Now 'a' has 2. Only the space and '!' are still wrong.
solutionLayers.check: Layer 3: the hard part comes back. Only letters and digits get counted.
solutionLayers.checkOutput: The right answer. Nothing from layer 1 was thrown away: each layer only added code.

charCodeRanges.title: Character codes: is it a letter or a digit?
charCodeRanges.start: Every character has a number. The digits, the capital letters and the lowercase letters each fill one block of numbers.
charCodeRanges.inside: {{char}} has code {{code}}. It's inside a green block: a letter or a digit.
charCodeRanges.outside: {{char}} has code {{code}}. It's outside every green block: not a letter or a digit.
charCodeRanges.summary: Three range checks answer the question, with no regular expression. Watch the edges: '[' is 91, one past 'Z', and '`' is 96, one before 'a'.

instances.title: One class, many cookies
instances.start: class Cookie is the cookie cutter: a shape you can use again and again. On its own, it isn't a cookie yet.
instances.first: new Cookie('chocolate') stamps out the first cookie, an instance named cookieOne, with its own flavor.
instances.second: The same cutter makes a second instance, cookieTwo. Same shape, different flavor.
instances.summary: One class, two instances. Each cookie keeps its own data, and you can stamp out as many as you need.

new.title: What new does, in four small steps
new.start: new Cookie('chocolate') looks like one action, but JavaScript does four things.
new.empty: 1. It makes a brand-new, empty object.
new.this: 2. It points this at that object, so the constructor knows which cookie it's building.
new.run: 3. It runs the constructor. this.flavor = 'chocolate' writes the flavor onto the new object.
new.returned: 4. It returns the finished object, and cookieOne now points to it.

methods.title: Getters and setters: each cookie answers for itself
methods.start: Two instances of the same class: cookieOne is chocolate and cookieTwo is vanilla.
methods.getOne: cookieOne.getFlavor() runs with this pointing at cookieOne, so it returns 'chocolate'.
methods.getTwo: Same method, called on cookieTwo: this is cookieTwo now, so it returns 'vanilla'.
methods.set: cookieOne.setFlavor('oatmeal') changes only cookieOne. cookieTwo isn't touched.
methods.getAgain: Reading it again shows the change: cookieOne.getFlavor() is now 'oatmeal'.
methods.summary: Getters read an instance's data and setters change it. Both work on this: whichever cookie you called them on.

listClassPreview.title: A preview: the LinkedList class at work
listClassPreview.create: new LinkedList('Ana') creates a list with one guest. The constructor sets everything up.
listClassPreview.push: push('Ben') adds a guest at the end.
listClassPreview.unshift: unshift('Zoe') adds a guest at the start.
listClassPreview.insert: insert(1, 'Cleo') puts a guest at index 1, between Zoe and Ana.
listClassPreview.remove: remove(1) takes out the guest at index 1: Cleo leaves.
listClassPreview.pop: pop() removes the last guest, Ben.
listClassPreview.shift: shift() removes the first guest, Zoe.
listClassPreview.summary: Each method did one specific job on the list. In the Linked Lists module you'll write every one of them yourself.

valueCopy.title: Copying a number copies the value
valueCopy.copy: let seats = guestCount copies the 5 into seats. Now there are two separate 5s.
valueCopy.change: guestCount = 8 changes only guestCount. seats still holds its own 5.
valueCopy.summary: seats is still 5. Numbers, strings and booleans are copied, so changing one variable never changes the other.

referenceCopy.title: Copying an object copies the arrow
referenceCopy.start: card doesn't hold the object itself: it holds an arrow to object A, { value: 'Ana' }.
referenceCopy.copy: let sameCard = card copies the arrow, not the object. Both variables now point to the same object A.
referenceCopy.change: card.value = 'Ben' follows card's arrow and changes object A.
referenceCopy.read: sameCard follows its arrow to the same object, so sameCard.value is 'Ben' too.
referenceCopy.summary: card === sameCard is true: they're the same object. There's still only one object A.

pointerMove.title: Moving pointers, and garbage collection
pointerMove.start: first points to object A, { value: 'Ana' }.
pointerMove.second: let second = first: second points to object A too.
pointerMove.third: let third = { value: 'Cleo' } makes a new object B, and third points to it.
pointerMove.moveSecond: second = third moves second's arrow to object B. Object A still has first.
pointerMove.moveFirst: first = third moves the last arrow away from A. Nothing points to object A any more, so nothing can reach it.
pointerMove.collected: JavaScript's garbage collector finds objects nothing points to and frees their memory. Object A is gone.

anatomy.title: The parts of a linked list
anatomy.line: Four guests in a conga line. Each one holds on to the next guest in line, and that's really all a linked list is.
anatomy.node: Each box is a node. A node holds one value, like 'Ben', plus a pointer to the node after it.
anatomy.next: That pointer is called next. Ana's next points to Ben: that's the link in "linked list".
anatomy.head: head points to the first node. Every trip through the list starts here.
anatomy.tail: tail points to the last node, so the end of the line is always one step away.
anatomy.null: Dev is last, so Dev's next is null: nothing comes after. A list that ends in null is called null-terminated.
anatomy.summary: To reach any guest, start at head and follow next, one node at a time, until you hit null.

costEnd.title: The back of the line: push is O(1), pop is O(n)
costEnd.start: A line of four guests. head is on Ana and tail is on Dev.
costEnd.newNode: push('Eve') starts with a new node for Eve. Nothing points to it yet.
costEnd.link: tail already points to Dev, so tail.next = newNode links Dev to Eve in one move.
costEnd.moveTail: tail = newNode moves tail onto Eve. Two moves, whether the line has 4 guests or 4,000: push is O(1).
costEnd.popProblem: Now pop() Eve. tail has to move back to Dev, and the only thing pointing at Dev is Cleo's next. We can't walk backwards from Eve.
costEnd.walkStart: So we start at head, with a pointer called temp. temp is on {{name}}. Is its next the tail? No.
costEnd.walk: temp moves to {{name}}. Its next still isn't the tail, so keep walking.
costEnd.walkFound: temp is on {{name}}, and its next is the tail. That's the new last guest.
costEnd.moveTailBack: tail = temp moves tail back to Dev.
costEnd.cut: tail.next = null cuts Eve off. Nothing points to Eve's node now.
costEnd.summary: pop had to walk the whole line to find the guest before the tail. The longer the line, the longer the walk: pop is O(n).

costFront.title: The front of the line: unshift and shift are O(1)
costFront.start: The same line: head on Ana, tail on Dev.
costFront.newNode: unshift('Zoe') starts with a new node for Zoe.
costFront.link: head already points to Ana, so newNode.next = head points Zoe at Ana. No walking.
costFront.moveHead: head = newNode moves head onto Zoe. Two moves, however long the line is: unshift is O(1).
costFront.shift: shift() is one move: head = head.next puts head back on Ana. Nothing points to Zoe now, so the garbage collector takes Zoe's node.
costFront.summary: At the front, head hands us the node we need right away. Adding and removing there never walks: both are O(1).

costMiddle.title: The middle of the line: insert and remove are O(n)
costMiddle.start: Let's insert Eve at index 3, between Cleo and Dev. There are no indexes to jump to, so we count while we walk.
costMiddle.walkStart: temp starts at head: {{name}} is index 0.
costMiddle.walkFound: temp moves to {{name}}: index 2, the node right before index 3. Stop here.
costMiddle.link: newNode.next = temp.next points Eve at Dev, the node Cleo points to. Link the new node first, so Dev isn't lost.
costMiddle.insert: temp.next = newNode points Cleo at Eve. Eve is in, at index 3. Linking took 2 moves, but the walk took 3 steps.
costMiddle.removeWalk: Now remove index 3 again. Same walk: temp stops on Cleo, at index 2.
costMiddle.remove: temp.next = temp.next.next points Cleo past Eve, straight to Dev. Nothing points to Eve, so Eve is gone.
costMiddle.summary: Moving the pointers is O(1), but the walk to the right spot grows with the line. Insert and remove are O(n).

costLookup.title: Finding a guest: O(n), by value or by index
costLookup.start: Find Cleo. A linked list can only start at head and look at one node at a time.
costLookup.check: Is {{name}} Cleo? No. Move to the next node.
costLookup.foundValue: Is {{name}} Cleo? Yes, after visiting 3 nodes. Finding by value is O(n).
costLookup.byIndex: Finding index 2 is no faster: count 0, 1, 2 while walking from head. Cleo again, after visiting 3 nodes.
costLookup.array: An array jumps straight to guests[2], whatever its length. That's O(1), and a linked list can't do it.
costLookup.summary: In a linked list, finding a guest by value or by index means walking: O(n) either way.

nodeClass.title: Four methods, one job in common

job.create: starts the list with a guest
job.push: adds a guest at the end
job.unshift: adds a guest at the front
job.insert: adds a guest at an index

nodeClass.create: The constructor gets a value and makes a node for it.
nodeClass.push: push gets a value and makes a node, then adds it at the end.
nodeClass.unshift: unshift gets a value and makes a node, then adds it at the front.
nodeClass.insert: insert gets a value and makes a node, then puts it at an index.
nodeClass.nodeClass: Four methods make the same thing. Instead of writing that code four times, we write it once, in its own class: Node.
nodeClass.newNode: Now any method makes a node in one line: new Node('Ana') gives { value: 'Ana', next: null }.

constructorExamples.title: Examples for the constructor
constructorExamples.one: One value: one node. head and tail both point to it, and length is 1.
constructorExamples.empty: No value: an empty list. head and tail point to null, and length is 0.
constructorExamples.zero: 0 is a real value, so it gets a node too. Only a missing value means "empty".
constructorExamples.many: Many guests? The constructor makes one node at most. push adds the rest, in the next lesson.

constructorPlan.title: The plan, as comments
constructorPlan.empty: Step 1: start empty. head and tail point to null, and length is 0.
constructorPlan.makeNode: Step 2a: if we got a value, make a new node with it. newNode points to it.
constructorPlan.head: Step 2b: point head at the new node.
constructorPlan.tail: Step 2c: point tail at the same node. head and tail now share one node.
constructorPlan.length: Step 2d: the length is 1. The list is ready.

comments.popProblem: pop: tail has to move back to Dev
comments.removeAt3: remove index 3: walk to index 2 again
comments.planEmpty: 1. start empty: head and tail are null, length is 0
comments.planMakeNode: 2a. a value was given: make a new node with it
comments.planHead: 2b. point head at the new node
comments.planTail: 2c. point tail at the same node
comments.push1: 1. make a new node with the value
comments.push2: 2. if the list is empty: head and tail both point to the new node
comments.push3: 3a. otherwise: the last node's next points to the new node
comments.push4: 3b. tail moves to the new node
comments.push5: 4. add 1 to length, 5. return the list
comments.pop1: 1. if the list is empty, return undefined
comments.pop2: 2. temp and pre both start at head
comments.pop3: 3. walk: while temp has a next, pre = temp, then temp moves on
comments.pop4: 4. tail moves to pre, and the new tail's next becomes null
comments.pop6: 6. if length is now 0, head and tail become null
comments.unshift1: 1. make a new node with the value
comments.unshift2: 2. if the list is empty: head and tail both point to the new node
comments.unshift3: 3a. otherwise: the new node's next points to the first node
comments.unshift4: 3b. head moves to the new node
comments.unshift5: 4. add 1 to length, 5. return the list
comments.shift1: 1. if the list is empty, return undefined
comments.shift2: 2. temp points to the first node
comments.shift3: 3. head moves to the next node
comments.shift4: 4. temp's next becomes null, to cut it off
comments.shift6: 6. if length is now 0, tail becomes null too
comments.get1: 1. if index < 0 or index >= length, return undefined
comments.get3: 3. move temp forward, index times: now at index {{index}}
comments.set1: 1. temp = this.get(index): the node, or undefined
comments.set2: 2. if temp is a node: change its value, return true
comments.insert1: 1. if index < 0 or index > length, return false
comments.insert2: 2. index 0? unshift. index === length? push. Then return true
comments.insert4: 4. temp = the node before the spot: this.get(index - 1)
comments.insert5: 5. the new node's next points to temp's next
comments.insert6: 6. temp's next points to the new node
comments.remove1: 1. if index < 0 or index >= length, return undefined
comments.remove2: 2. index 0? shift. Last index? pop. Return what they return
comments.remove3: 3. before = the node before the spot: this.get(index - 1)
comments.remove4: 4. temp = before.next: the node that leaves
comments.remove6: 6. temp's next becomes null, to cut it off
comments.reverse1: 1. swap head and tail (temp remembers the old head)
comments.reverse2: 2. prev starts as null, and so does next
comments.reverse3: 3. for each node: next = temp.next, to remember the rest
comments.reverse5: 5. prev = temp, then temp = next: both move one node on
comments.reverse6: 6. after the last node, return the list

push.title: push: add a guest at the back
push.start: A line of three guests: head on Ana, tail on Cleo, length 3.
push.call: push('Dev') adds a node for Dev after the tail. tail moves to Dev, and length goes up to 4.
push.returns: push returns this, the whole list, so you can keep using it right away.

pushExamples.title: Examples for push: empty, one guest, many guests
pushExamples.emptyBefore: Example 1: an empty line. head and tail are both null.
pushExamples.emptyAfter: There's no last node to link from, so head and tail both point to Ana's new node. length is 1.
pushExamples.oneBefore: Example 2: one guest. head and tail are both on Ana.
pushExamples.oneAfter: Ana's next points to Ben, and tail moves to Ben. head stays on Ana.
pushExamples.manyBefore: Example 3: three guests, with tail on Cleo.
pushExamples.manyAfter: The same two moves: Cleo's next points to Dev, then tail moves to Dev. Nobody else is touched.

pushPlan.title: push's plan, as comments
pushPlan.makeNode: Step 1: make a new node for Dev. newNode points to it, but nothing in the line does yet.
pushPlan.notEmpty: Step 2: is the line empty? No, head is on Ana, so this step doesn't apply.
pushPlan.link: Step 3a: the last node, Cleo, points its next at the new node.
pushPlan.moveTail: Step 3b: tail moves to the new node. Dev is the last guest now.
pushPlan.length: Steps 4 and 5: length goes up to 4, and push returns the list.
pushPlan.emptyCase: On an empty line, step 2 does the whole job: head and tail both point to the new node.

pop.title: pop: remove the guest at the back
pop.start: A line of four guests: head on Ana, tail on Dev.
pop.call: pop() cuts Dev's node off the end. tail moves back to Cleo, and length goes down to 3.
pop.returns: pop returns the node it removed, so you know who left.

popExamples.title: Examples for pop: empty, one guest, many guests
popExamples.emptyBefore: Example 1: an empty line. There's nobody to pop.
popExamples.emptyAfter: pop() returns undefined, and the line stays empty.
popExamples.oneBefore: Example 2: one guest. head and tail are both on Ana.
popExamples.oneAfter: Popping the only guest empties the line: head and tail both go back to null, and length is 0.
popExamples.manyBefore: Example 3: three guests, with tail on Cleo.
popExamples.manyAfter: Cleo's node is cut off and returned. tail moves back to Ben, the guest before.

popPlan.title: pop's plan, as comments
popPlan.notEmpty: Step 1: is the line empty? No, so there's someone to pop.
popPlan.start: Step 2: temp and pre both start at head, on Ana.
popPlan.walk: Step 3: walk until temp has no next. temp ends on Cleo, the last guest, and pre on Ben, the one before.
popPlan.moveTail: Step 4: tail moves to pre, Ben, and Ben's next becomes null. Cleo is out of the line.
popPlan.oneLeft: Step 6 matters with one guest: after popping Ana, length is 0, so head and tail must become null too.
popPlan.returnTemp: Step 7: return temp, Cleo's node: the guest who left.

unshift.title: unshift: add a guest at the front
unshift.start: A line of three guests: head on Ana, tail on Cleo.
unshift.call: unshift('Zoe') adds a node for Zoe before Ana. head moves to Zoe, and length goes up to 4.
unshift.returns: unshift returns this, the whole list, just like push.

unshiftExamples.title: Examples for unshift: empty, one guest, many guests
unshiftExamples.emptyBefore: Example 1: an empty line. head and tail are both null.
unshiftExamples.emptyAfter: With nobody in line, Zoe is first and last: head and tail both point to Zoe's node.
unshiftExamples.oneAfter: Zoe's next points to Ana, and head moves to Zoe. tail stays on Ana.
unshiftExamples.manyBefore: Example 3: three guests, with head on Ana.
unshiftExamples.manyAfter: The same two moves: Zoe points to Ana, then head moves to Zoe. Nobody else moves.

unshiftPlan.title: unshift's plan, as comments
unshiftPlan.makeNode: Step 1: make a new node for Zoe. Nothing in the line points to it yet.
unshiftPlan.notEmpty: Step 2: is the line empty? No, head is on Ana, so this step doesn't apply.
unshiftPlan.link: Step 3a: the new node's next points to Ana, the node head is on.
unshiftPlan.moveHead: Step 3b: head moves to the new node. Zoe is first now.
unshiftPlan.length: Steps 4 and 5: length goes up to 4, and unshift returns the list.
unshiftPlan.emptyCase: On an empty line, step 2 does the whole job: head and tail both point to the new node.

shift.title: shift: remove the guest at the front
shift.start: A line of three guests: head on Ana, tail on Cleo.
shift.call: shift() takes Ana's node off the front. head moves to Ben, and length goes down to 2.
shift.returns: shift returns the node it removed, cut off from the rest of the line.

shiftExamples.title: Examples for shift: empty, one guest, many guests
shiftExamples.emptyBefore: Example 1: an empty line. There's nobody to shift.
shiftExamples.emptyAfter: shift() returns undefined, and the line stays empty.
shiftExamples.oneAfter: Shifting the only guest empties the line: head becomes null, and tail has to become null too.
shiftExamples.manyBefore: Example 3: three guests, with head on Ana.
shiftExamples.manyAfter: Ana's node comes off the front and is returned. head moves to Ben, and tail stays on Cleo.

shiftPlan.title: shift's plan, as comments
shiftPlan.notEmpty: Step 1: is the line empty? No, so there's someone to shift.
shiftPlan.temp: Step 2: temp points to the first node, Ana's, so we can still return it at the end.
shiftPlan.moveHead: Step 3: head moves to the next node, Ben. Ana's node is out of the line, but it still points to Ben.
shiftPlan.cut: Step 4: Ana's next becomes null. Now the node we return doesn't drag anybody along.
shiftPlan.oneLeft: Step 6 matters with one guest: once Ana leaves, length is 0, so tail must become null too.

get.title: get: find the node at an index
get.start: A line of four guests. Indexes count from head: Ana is 0, Ben 1, Cleo 2 and Dev 3.
get.call: get(2) starts at head and moves forward 2 times, counting: Ana (0), Ben (1), Cleo (2).
get.returns: It returns Cleo's node, still in the line. The list doesn't change.

getExamples.title: Examples for get: empty, one guest, the last guest, out of range
getExamples.empty: An empty line has no index 0, so get(0) returns undefined.
getExamples.one: With one guest, 0 is the only valid index: get(0) returns Ana's node right away, with no moves.
getExamples.last: get(3) on four guests walks the whole line to Dev, the last index: length - 1.
getExamples.negative: Index -1 doesn't exist: get returns undefined without walking.
getExamples.tooBig: Index 4 doesn't exist either: the last index is 3 (length - 1). get returns undefined.

getPlan.title: get's plan, as comments
getPlan.check: Step 1: is 2 in range? It isn't below 0, and it's below the length, 4. Yes.
getPlan.start: Step 2: temp starts at head: index 0.
getPlan.move: Step 3: one move forward, and temp is on index 1.
getPlan.arrive: Another move: index 2. Index 2 takes 2 moves.

set.title: set: change the value at an index
set.start: A line of four guests. Ben's name tag should really say Benny.
set.call: set(1, 'Benny') finds the node at index 1 and changes its value. No node is added or removed.
set.returns: set returns true: the change worked.

setExamples.title: Examples for set: in range, out of range, empty
setExamples.inRange: set(3, 'Devon') finds index 3 and changes Dev to Devon. It returns true.
setExamples.outOfRange: set(9, 'Zoe'): there's no index 9, so nothing changes. It returns false.
setExamples.empty: On an empty line, no index is valid, so set returns false.

setPlan.title: set's plan, as comments
setPlan.get: Step 1: let get do the finding. this.get(1) gives back Ben's node.
setPlan.change: Step 2: temp is a node, so its value changes to 'Benny', and set returns true.
setPlan.missing: Step 3: with index 9, get gives back undefined, so set returns false.

insert.title: insert: add a guest at an index
insert.call: insert(2, 'Eve') puts a new node for Eve at index 2, between Ben and Cleo. Cleo and Dev move up to indexes 3 and 4.
insert.returns: insert returns true: the new guest is in.

insertExamples.title: Examples for insert: front, back, middle, out of range
insertExamples.front: Index 0 is the front of the line: that's exactly what unshift does.
insertExamples.back: Index 4, the length, is the spot right after the last guest: that's exactly what push does.
insertExamples.middle: Index 2 is in the middle: walk to the node before it and link Eve in.
insertExamples.outOfRange: Index 7 is past the end, with a gap no node could fill: insert returns false and changes nothing.

insertPlan.title: insert's plan, as comments
insertPlan.check: Step 1: is 2 between 0 and the length, 4? Yes.
insertPlan.notEnds: Step 2: 2 isn't 0 and isn't 4, so neither unshift nor push fits.
insertPlan.makeNode: Step 3: make a new node for Eve.
insertPlan.before: Step 4: get(1) walks to Ben, the node right before index 2.
insertPlan.linkNew: Step 5: Eve's next points to Cleo, the node Ben points to. Link the new node first, so Cleo isn't lost.
insertPlan.linkBefore: Step 6: Ben's next points to Eve. Eve is in the line, at index 2.
insertPlan.length: Step 7: length goes up to 5, and insert returns true.

remove.title: remove: take out the guest at an index
remove.call: remove(2) takes Cleo's node out of the middle. Ben now points straight to Dev, and length goes down to 3.
remove.returns: remove returns the node it took out, cut off from the line.

removeExamples.title: Examples for remove: front, back, middle, out of range
removeExamples.front: Index 0 is the front of the line: that's shift.
removeExamples.back: Index 3, the last one (length - 1), is the back: that's pop.
removeExamples.middle: Index 2 is in the middle: point the node before it past it.
removeExamples.outOfRange: Index 4 doesn't exist: remove returns undefined.

removePlan.title: remove's plan, as comments
removePlan.check: Step 1: is 2 in range, from 0 to 3? Yes.
removePlan.notEnds: Step 2: 2 isn't 0 and isn't the last index, 3, so neither shift nor pop fits.
removePlan.before: Step 3: get(1) walks to Ben, the node before index 2.
removePlan.temp: Step 4: temp = Ben's next, Cleo: the node that leaves. No second walk needed.
removePlan.skip: Step 5: Ben's next skips Cleo and points to Dev. Cleo is out of the line, but still points to Dev.
removePlan.cut: Step 6: Cleo's next becomes null, so the node we return comes alone.
removePlan.length: Step 7: length goes down to 3, and remove returns Cleo's node.

reverse.title: reverse: turn the line around
reverse.start: A line of four guests: head on Ana, tail on Dev, and every arrow pointing right.
reverse.call: reverse() swaps head and tail and flips every arrow. Now head is on Dev, and every arrow points left.
reverse.returns: Read from head, the line is Dev, Cleo, Ben, Ana. reverse returns the list.

reverseExamples.title: Examples for reverse: empty, one guest, two, many
reverseExamples.empty: An empty line reversed is still empty.
reverseExamples.one: One guest reversed is the same line: head and tail are both on Ana.
reverseExamples.twoAfter: Reversed: Ben, then Ana. head and tail swap, and Ben now points to Ana.
reverseExamples.many: Four guests: Dev, Cleo, Ben, Ana. Every node points to the one that used to come before it.

reversePlan.title: reverse's plan, as comments
reversePlan.swap: Step 1: swap head and tail. temp keeps the old head, Ana, so the loop can start there.
reversePlan.start: Step 2: prev starts as null, behind Ana. next will hold on to the rest of the line.
reversePlan.remember: Step 3: next = Ana's next, Ben. Now the rest of the line has a pointer on it.
reversePlan.flip: Step 4: Ana's next flips to prev, null. There's a gap between Ana and Ben now, but next still holds Ben.
reversePlan.step: Step 5: prev moves to Ana, and temp crosses the gap to Ben. Steps 3 to 5 repeat for every node.
reversePlan.repeat: After 4 rounds, every arrow points left, temp is null, and prev is on Dev, the new first node.

arrayVsLinkedList.title: From an array to a linked list
arrayVsLinkedList.array: An array of four guests. Every guest has an index, from 0 to 3.
arrayVsLinkedList.arrayMemory: In memory, an array's items sit side by side, in one block. That's how guests[2] jumps straight there: the start of the block, plus 2.
arrayVsLinkedList.noIndexes: A linked list drops the indexes. There's no guests[2] any more.
arrayVsLinkedList.listMemory: Its nodes don't sit side by side either: they can be anywhere in memory. Each node remembers where the next one is.
arrayVsLinkedList.chain: So we draw it as a chain. head points to the first node, every node points to the one after it, and the final node points to null.

linkedListBigO.title: Linked lists vs arrays, side by side
linkedListBigO.all: Every operation from this lesson, for both data structures.
linkedListBigO.ties: Half the rows are a tie: push, insert, remove and finding by value cost the same in both.
linkedListBigO.arrays: Arrays win two rows: pop and finding by index are O(1) for an array, O(n) for a linked list.
linkedListBigO.lists: Linked lists win two rows: adding and removing at the front are O(1), while an array re-indexes every item.
linkedListBigO.summary: Neither one wins every row. Pick the one that's fast at what you'll do most.

node.title: A closer look at one node
node.node: Let's take one node out of the line: Dev's node. We draw it as a box with an arrow.
node.value: Part one is the value: 'Dev'. But the value alone isn't the node.
node.next: Part two is next, the pointer. Dev is the last guest, so next is null.
node.whole: The node is the whole thing, value and next together: one object, { value: 'Dev', next: null }.

nested.title: The list is objects inside objects
nested.dev: Start with the last guest: Dev's node, with next set to null.
nested.cleo: Cleo's next is set to Dev's node. In code, Dev's whole object now sits inside Cleo's next: that's the arrow.
nested.ben: Ben's next is set to Cleo's node, so Cleo and Dev are both inside Ben now.
nested.ana: Ana's node holds all the others. head points to it: the outermost object.
nested.tail: tail points to the innermost object, Dev's node. We pointed it there by setting it equal to Cleo's next.
nested.summary: The boxes and arrows and the nested objects are the same list, drawn two ways.
